children: said two additional analyses of its late-stage REDEFINE 1 trial found differing weight-loss patterns and improvements in daily functioning among adults receiving its experimental obesity treatment CagriSema.

For investors, the findings add evidence that could help Novo position the drug commercially if approved. However, they are exploratory analyses conducted after the trial, rather than definitive new tests of effectiveness. Novo
said a U.S. regulatory decision is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

CagriSema is a weekly injection combining cagrilintide and semaglutide, medicines that mimic hormones involved in appetite regulation. The trial enrolled adults with obesity, or overweight and related health conditions, without type 2 diabetes.

Among CagriSema recipients analyzed, 67.8% lost at least 5% of their weight within eight weeks. These early responders averaged 25.4% weight loss at week 68, compared with 17.8% among slower responders. The figures used measurements collected while participants were receiving treatment and should not guide changes in clinical decisions, the announcement said.

A separate questionnaire analysis found 73.1% reported meaningful improvement in everyday physical activities, versus 49.1% receiving placebo. Improvements in self-esteem and social comfort were reported by 69%, versus 42.1%. Those estimates assumed everyone followed treatment as intended.
Digestive side effects affected 79.6% of CagriSema recipients, versus 39.9% on placebo. Treatment discontinuation because of side effects occurred in 5.9% and 3.5%, respectively.
presented the analyses at ObesityWeek 2026. CagriSema remains unapproved in the United States, according to the announcement.

title: Novo Nordisk reports additional CagriSema weight-loss findings
